title: Week 2 · Simple made easy
subtitle: Rich Hickey: Simple Made Easy · The Value of Values · Hammock Driven Development
author: Medhat

slides.title: Simple made easy
slides.subtitle: Track B · Week 2 — Simplicity, values, and thinking
slides.date: Rich Hickey × 3: Simple Made Easy · The Value of Values · Hammock Driven Development
notes: Week 2 of Track B. Three talks by one speaker, taken as lectures.
Quotes are verbatim from the community transcripts at github.com/matthiasn/talk-transcripts.

slides.title: Week 2

items.text: Simple vs easy, complecting, value-oriented design, deliberate design time
Rich Hickey, Simple Made Easy (2011)
Rich Hickey, The Value of Values (2012)
Rich Hickey, Hammock Driven Development (2010)
Three places where code confused “easy” with “simple”, and what untangling costs now

slides.notes: From the track document: “Take notes as if they were lectures, because they are.”

slides.title: Where Week 1 left us

items.text: Ousterhout: complexity is whatever makes a system hard to understand and modify
sub: “Complexity is anything related to the structure of a software system that makes it hard to understand and modify the system.”

items.text: Parnas: hide each decision that is likely to change
Moseley & Marks: most of it is accidental, and mostly state
sub: “the major contributor to this complexity in many systems is the handling of state”

items.text: Open question: is there an objective test for “complex”?

slides.notes: Ousterhout's definition is about a reader's experience. Hickey offers one you can check by looking at the code: is anything braided together?

slides.title: Three talks, one argument

items.text: 2011 · Simple Made Easy: a vocabulary — simple is objective, easy is relative
2012 · The Value of Values: the biggest braid is place — use values and facts
2010 · Hammock Driven Development: none of it happens without time to think

slides.notes: Not in chronological order: the vocabulary first, then its main application, then the practice that makes it possible.

slides.source: the first slide of Simple Made Easy
slides.notes: “We need to build simple systems if we want to build good systems. I do not think we focus enough on that.”

slides.title: Two words we use as one

left.name: Simple
points: sim-plex: one fold, one braid — opposite: complex
one role, one task, one concept, one dimension
About lack of interleaving, not cardinality
Objective: you can go and look for the braids

right.name: Easy
points: adjacens: to lie near — opposite: hard
near at hand: installed, in the toolkit
near our understanding: familiar · near our capabilities
Relative: easy for whom?

notes: “What matters for simplicity is that there is no interleaving, not that there is only one thing.”
He admits the last step of the “easy” etymology is speculative: “I bought it because it serves this talk really well”

slides.title: Easy is relative
items: “Now I cannot read German. Does that mean German is unreadable? No. I do not know German.”
“if you want everything to be familiar, you will never learn anything new”
“easy is always going to be: easy for whom, or hard for whom?”

items.text: How the words get swapped:
sub: “‘Oh, I like to use that technology because it is simple,’ and when I am saying simple, I mean easy.”

slides.notes: The third sense of easy — near our capabilities — is the one we avoid talking about: “due to a combination of hubris and insecurity, we never really talk about whether or not something is outside of our capabilities.”

slides.title: Constructs vs artifacts

items.text: “We program with constructs.”
sub: languages, libraries, the code as we type it

items.text: “But we are in a business of artifacts.”
sub: the running program: quality, correctness, maintenance, change

items.text: We judge the construct by how it feels to type
sub: “Oh, look; I only had to type 16 characters. Wow! That is great.”

items.text: Employers like the first two kinds of easy too
sub: “They just care that somebody can go sit in your seat, start typing.”

items: “We must assess constructs by their artifacts”
slides.notes: This is the distinction behind the whole talk: ease is a property of the authoring experience, simplicity a property of what you ship.

slides.title: Limits
items: “We can only hope to make reliable those things we can understand”
“We can only consider a few things at a time”
“Intertwined things must be considered together”
“Complexity undermines understanding”
slides.notes: “every intertwining is adding this burden, and the burden is kind of combinatorial as to the number of things that we can consider.”

slides.title: What's true of every bug in the field?
slides.context: Hickey on change and debugging: you can't change or fix what you can't reason about. He asks the room a question.

lines.text: And I like to ask this question: what is true of every bug found in the field?
It got written. Yes. What is a more interesting fact about it? It passed the type checker.
It passed all the tests. OK. So now what do you do? I think we are in this world I would like to call guardrail programming.

slides.notes: “Your ability to reason about your program is critical to debugging”

slides.quote: Who drives their car around banging against the guardrail saying, "Whoa! I am glad I have got these guardrails because I would never make it to the show on time."
notes: “Do guardrails guide you places? No.”
Not “don't test”: tests and types are safety nets. They don't point the car anywhere.

slides.title: Sprinters
slides.context: On development speed: “But I have all this speed. I am agile. I am fast.”

lines.text: What kind of runner can run as fast as they possibly can from the very start of a race?
Only somebody who runs really short races, OK?
But of course, we are programmers, and we are smarter than runners, apparently, because we know how to fix that problem. We just fire the starting pistol every hundred yards and call it a new sprint.

slides.title: Easy gives early speed
slides.caption: if you ignore complexity, you will slow down. You will invariably slow down over the long haul.
notes: His chart plots speed (easy starts high and drops; simple starts lower and climbs). This one plots its running total — the same story, drawn like APOSD figure 3.1 from Week 1.
“this is my really scientific graph. You notice how none of the axes are -- there is no numbers on it because I just completely made it up.”
Why can't simple go fast from the start? “You have to think.”

slides.title: Easy yet complex

items.text: Many complicating constructs are
sub: succinctly described · familiar · available · easy to use

items: “What matters is the complexity they yield”

items.text: Complexity you chose, not the problem's, is incidental
sub: “incidental is Latin for ‘your fault’.”

items: “are you programming with a loom?”
slides.notes: “Is having a test suite and refactoring tools going to make changing the knitted castle faster than changing the Lego castle? No way.”

slides.title: Making things easy

items.text: Near at hand: install it, get it approved
Familiar: learn it, try it
Near our capabilities?
sub: “We are not going to move our brain closer to the complexity. We have to make things near by simplifying them.”

items.text: Jugglers: three balls on average, nine or twelve at the very best
sub: “How many of those balls do you want to be incidental complexity and how many do you want to be problem complexity?”

slides.notes: “Compared to the complexity we can create, we are all statistically at the same point in our ability to understand it, which is not very good.”

slides.title: His own example: parens are hard

items.text: Not at hand: no editor support for structural editing
Not familiar: parens on the other side of the verb
But are they simple? Not in Common Lisp or Scheme
sub: “Parens wrap calls. They wrap grouping. They wrap data structures.”

items.text: The fix is more things, not fewer: add a data structure (Clojure's vectors)
sub: “now the simplicity is back in the construct, and it is just a familiarity thing, which you can solve for yourself.”

slides.notes: The first two complaints are about ease and are the learner's job. The third is a real complexity complaint and the language designer's fault — overloading one construct for three jobs is complecting.

slides.quote: LISP programmers know the value of everything and the cost of nothing.
notes: Hickey lifts it to all of us: “You never see in these discussions: was there a tradeoff? Is there any downside? Is there anything bad that comes along with this? Never.”

slides.title: Complect vs compose

left.name: complect
points: “To interleave, entwine, braid”
“Complecting things is the source of complexity”
“Best to avoid in the first place”

right.name: compose
points: “To place together”
“Composing simple components is the key to robust software”
Lego, not knitting

notes: “Complect” is archaic, chosen because braid and entwine have no good/bad connotation: “Complect is obviously bad.”
“It is the same stuff in both those diagrams. It is the same strips! What happened? They got complected.”

slides.title: Modular isn't simple

layouts.label: (a) two blocks, no calls between them
(b) each thinks only about the studs

slides.caption: Partitioning and stratification don't imply simplicity
notes: His three Lego slides: two blocks; then each with a thought balloon of the other; then each thinking only of the other's studs.
“You can write modular software with all kinds of interconnections between them. They may not call each other, but they are completely complected.”
This is Parnas's test from Week 1 with Hickey's picture: count who must change.

slides.quote: Then you get out in the field and you are like, oh, my God! This thing presumes that that thing never returns the number 17.
slides.notes: “I would encourage you to be particularly careful not to be fooled by code organization.”

slides.title: State complects value and time

runs.caption: The variable is private. The complexity isn't.

slides.caption: Every machine downstream now depends on when you asked.
notes: “if every time you call that method with the same arguments, you can get a different result, guess what happened? That complexity just leaked right out of there.”
An invented example: a pricing step that remembers whether the welcome discount was used.

slides.title: State is never simple
items: “Complects value and time”

items.text: “It is easy, in the at-hand and familiar senses”
“Interweaves everything that touches it, directly or indirectly”
sub: “Not mitigated by modules, encapsulation”

items.text: The only way out is a functional interface
sub: “same input, same output.”

items: “This is not about concurrency.”
notes: “It is like dropping some dark liquid into a vase. It is just going to end up all over the place.”

Moseley & Marks (Week 1) say the same thing about testing: “a test (of any kind) that uses one particular set of inputs tells you nothing at all about the behaviour of the system or component when it is given a different set of inputs.”

slides.title: What each construct complects

items.text: State
sub: everything that touches it

items.text: Objects
sub: state, identity, value

items.text: Methods
sub: function and state, namespaces

items.text: Syntax
sub: meaning, order

items.text: Inheritance
sub: types

items.text: Switch / matching
sub: multiple who/what pairs

slides.notes: The left half of “The Complexity Toolkit” slide.

slides.title: …and the rest

items.text: var(iable)s
sub: value, time

items.text: Imperative loops, fold
sub: what / how — fold implies an order

items.text: Actors
sub: what / who

items.text: ORM
sub: OMG

items.text: Conditionals
sub: why, and the rest of the program

slides.notes: “object relational mapping has ‘oh, my God’ complecting going on. You cannot even begin to talk about how bad it is.”

slides.title: What's in your toolkit?

left.name: Complexity
points: State, objects · methods · vars
Inheritance, switch, matching
Syntax · imperative loops, fold
Actors · ORM · conditionals · inconsistency

right.name: Simplicity
points: Values (final, persistent collections) · functions, namespaces · managed refs
Polymorphism à la carte (protocols, type classes)
Data (maps, arrays, sets, JSON) · set functions
Queues · declarative data manipulation (SQL, Datalog) · rules · consistency (transactions, values)

notes: “The simplicity column just means simpler.”
“we can create precisely the same programs we are creating right now with these tools of complexity, with dramatically drastically simpler tools.”

slides.title: Designing simple things: abstract, don't hide

items.text: Abstract means drawn away — not “hiding stuff”
sub: “That is not what abstraction is, and that is not going to help you in this space.”

items.text: Take a job apart with six questions
sub: who · what · when · where · why · how

items.text: “I don't know, I don't want to know”
sub: a student made him a shirt: a Booch diagram where every line said it

slides.notes: “I don't want to know” is Parnas's information hiding from Week 1, as a habit.

slides.title: Who, what, how, when, where, why

items.text: Operations: small sets of functions, as specifications
sub: “Strictly separating ‘what’ from ‘how’ is the key to making ‘how’ somebody else's problem.”

items.text: Entities built from many subcomponents, passed in
Implementations as islands, joined by polymorphism
Don't let callers know where or when
sub: “if thing A calls thing B, you just complected it.”
“Stick a queue in there.”

items.text: Policy and rules, usually strewn through conditionals

slides.notes: “If you go in saying, ‘this is a job, and I have done who, what, when, where, why,’ and I found five components, do not feel bad. That is great.”

slides.title: More things, hanging straight

layouts.label: (a) A calls B; rules live in conditionals
(b) who / what / how / when / why apart

slides.caption: Simplicity often means making more things, not fewer
notes: An invented checkout to make the slide concrete. (b) has more modules and every change touches one.
“I would rather have more things hanging nice, straight down, not twisted together, than just a couple of things tied in a knot.”

slides.title: Information is simple
items: “The only thing you can possibly do with information is ruin it.”

items.text: Don't hide it behind a micro-language
sub: a class with information-specific methods
it thwarts generic data composition and ties logic to the representation du jour

items.text: Objects were for I/O devices
sub: “They were never supposed to be applied to information.”

items: “Represent data as data”
slides.notes: “Please start using maps and sets directly. Don't feel like I have to write a class now because I have a new piece of information.”

slides.title: Simplicity is a choice
items: “It is your fault if you do not have a simple system.”

items.text: “Your sensibilities about simplicity being equal to ease of use are wrong.”
sub: “You have to have entanglement radar.”

items.text: Testing, refactoring and type systems don't care
sub: “They are safety nets, but they are nothing more than that.”

items.text: Simplicity made easy
sub: choose simple constructs: It's the artifacts, not the authoring
create abstractions with simplicity as a basis
simplify the problem space before you start

slides.notes: “You want to start seeing interconnections between things that could be independent. That is where you are going to get the most power.”

slides.title: The Value of Values
slides.subtitle: Rich Hickey · JaxConf, July 2012 (the 30-minute keynote)
slides.notes: There is also an hour-long version (GOTO 2012); the transcript used here is the JaxConf keynote.

slides.title: What is a fact?
items: “Place where specific information is stored”
“There is a place for every piece of information”
“Facts have operations, e.g. get and set”
“Operations control how facts can change”
“To convey a fact, convey its location”

sticky.text: “Everything that I just said was wrong. Dead wrong.”

notes: “How many people are uncomfortable right now?”
Let the room sit with it before the last click.

slides.title: PLOP: place-oriented programming

items.text: Mutable objects are abstractions of places; tables, documents and records are places
sub: “any time new information replaces old information, you are doing Place-Oriented Programming.”

items.text: “Born of limitations of early computers”
sub: four kilowords of memory: you knew which addresses held the jump table

items.text: “Those limitations are long gone”
sub: “the capacity of these two things have increased a million-fold.”

items: “So why does PLOP still rule?”
slides.notes: “It totally made sense. And the key word there, the key aspect of that is: it made sense. It used to make sense.”

slides.title: Memory and records, before computers

items.text: Memory is open and associative
sub: “If your friend gets a new email address, that does not go into your brain and find your friend's email address cells”

items.text: Records endure and accrete
sub: “We did not go and smooth over the marble and chisel new stuff.”

items.text: Accountants never used erasers
sub: “They only made correcting entries.”

slides.notes: “we have now been doing this for so long that we believe our own myths about what these things mean.”

slides.title: Hickey's poll
slides.question: Is a string a value?
notes: “You always wait for ‘it depends,’ right? It is the best answer, so you hold out for it.”
“Is it immutable? If the string is immutable, it is a value. If it is not immutable, it is not a value.”
“How many people want to go back? No.”

slides.title: Values, in programming

items.text: Immutable
Semantically transparent
sub: “A value is about saying, ‘Compare me to something else. I am telling you what my precise meaning or significance is.’”

items.text: Equality and comparison are where logic starts
sub: “comparability is where we derive our ability to do logic, and to make decisions.”

slides.notes: “Value is not about encapsulating something in methods, and doing things.”

slides.title: The value propositions, in the small

items.text: Values can be shared
sub: neither side has to worry about the other

items.text: Reproducible results
sub: “If you define a function in terms of places, every time you are on that function, will you get the same answer? No.”

items.text: Easy to fabricate
sub: “Can I make an instance of your fancy interface in any other language? No.”

items.text: Language independent, generic
sub: “More code equals more bugs.”

items.text: Values aggregate to values
sub: an immutable collection of values is itself a value

slides.notes: “Objects were supposed to support reuse. They have done the exact opposite thing, especially in typed languages.”

slides.title: Aggregates

left.name: objects
points: Each class needs a locking policy and cloning semantics
Combine them and the policies don't combine
“It all falls away.”

right.name: values
points: No locks: nothing can change
No cloning: just keep the reference
“Values aggregate to values. All the benefits apply to aggregates.”

slides.notes: “It is like there is this napkin and on it, we have defined how we are going to use this object.”

slides.title: The value propositions, in the large

items.text: Conveyance
sub: “If I see something interesting and I communicate to you the place where I saw it, what have I actually conveyed to you? Nothing, right?”

items.text: Perception
sub: to look at many places at once you have to stop the world

items.text: Memory
sub: “Clone it. How do you do that? It depends. Exactly. It depends.”

items.text: “Values make the best interfaces”
sub: we already send JSON over the wire, not objects

items.text: Reduced coordination · location flexibility
sub: move a part to another thread, language or box

slides.notes: “In the large, we communicate values. But in the small, in a programming language, we start doing icky things.”

slides.title: Same facts, two systems

runs.caption: A friend changes their email address. Each fact rides on to the ledger.

states: Jan old · Mar new · Jun work
runs.caption: And again.
Open them up: one remembers only the most recent fact.

slides.caption: You cannot update a fact
notes: “the reason why you cannot update a fact is because you cannot change the past.”

The line itself is a nice picture of his other point: every program has a machine part (the belt and stations) and an information part (what rides the belt). Machines are fine for process; information should be values.

slides.title: Facts are values

items.text: Facts incorporate time
sub: “A fact is something that happened. It is not a place.”

items.text: Knowledge comes from comparing and combining facts
sub: especially from different points in time: trends, rates, totals

items.text: Most systems keep only the most recent facts
sub: “Imagine if you only knew the present value of any property or attribute in the world. How good would your decision making capability be?”

items.text: “Place has no role in an information model”

slides.notes: “information is not a little machine. It is not at all like a machine, and so you have to separate out these process constructs.”

slides.title: Programmer I.T.: we already know

items.text: Source control
sub: Update in place? — No.  Timestamps? — Of course!

items.text: Logs
sub: “Anyone use a log that says: the last latency was five?”

items.text: “Big data”
sub: the business to programmers: “That database you have, I like better than the one you gave me.”

slides.notes: “We are already... we are in the space age for ourselves, but we need to be in the space age for the businesses we are supporting.”

slides.title: The space age

items.text: Space: place and time together
sub: “If S3 never fills up, that is not the cloud, that is space.”

items.text: “new facts require new space”
sub: “This should be the end of Place-Oriented Programming.”

items.text: “If you could afford to do this, why would you do anything else?”
sub: “There will be garbage.”

slides.notes: “What I would recommend is that you try to take an information-oriented approach to the way you build your programs.”

slides.title: Hammock Driven Development
slides.subtitle: Rich Hickey · Clojure/conj, October 2010
slides.notes: Its first title was “Step Away from the Computer”. Other titles on his slides: “If We're Not Solving Problems, What are We Doing?” and “What Rich Does When He's Not Writing Tests”. He calls it an experience report, not science.

slides.title: When was the last time you…

items.text: “Thought hard about something for an hour”
sub: a day? over the course of a month? a year?

items: “Felt confident implementing something for the first time?”
slides.notes: “I consider myself extremely lucky to have had the ability to think about probably three different things for a year or more. One of them was Clojure.”

slides.title: Where bugs are cheapest

items.text: “Most expensive in production”
“Expensive in QA”
“Cheaper to fix in dev”
“Least expensive to avoid in design”
The biggest problems are problems of misconception, not implementation
sub: “There are not really type systems that can tell us if we have got a good idea, or what we are doing addresses that idea.”

slides.notes: “We do not have a good idea of what we are doing before we do it.”

slides.title: Analysis and design, simplified

items.text: Not UML, not the waterfall: two things
sub: identify the problem you're trying to solve
assess whether your solution solves it

items.text: “We should be solving problems. We should not be building features.”
sub: “Features are results, not objectives”

items: “Avoiding problems != solving them”

items.text: Problem solving is a skill you can practice
sub: Pólya, How to Solve It (1945)
“Practice methodology X” → get good at methodology X

slides.notes: “I would like you to ask yourself, where do you think there is more leverage? I do not care what X is.”

slides.title: The steps

items.text: State the problem — out loud, or (heaven forbid) write it down
What do you know? What don't you know? Related problems?
sub: “‘We have this problem. We need a NoSQL database.’ We have not actually said why.”

items.text: Find the problems in your solutions, and solve those too
Read in and around your space; look critically at other solutions
Enumerate two or more solutions, with their attributes and deficits

slides.notes: Each step ends the same way on his slides: write it down.

slides.quote: There should be question marks on that page. If there are no question marks, you are missing this step.
slides.notes: Stu Halloway's name for Hickey's design notes: the “document of despair”. Hickey: “It is not despairing. It is positive.”

slides.quote: Usually when they talk about tradeoffs in their software, they are talking about the parts of their software that suck. I had to make these tradeoffs. That is not what a tradeoff is, right?
slides.notes: “You have to look at, at least, two solutions to your problem. At least two.”

slides.title: Two minds

left.name: waking mind
points: Good at critical thinking: analysis, tactics
“Prone to finding local maxima”
Picks apart what the background mind brings back

right.name: background mind
points: Good at making connections: synthesis, strategy
Abstracts and draws analogies
“Unfortunately you can only feed it” — not direct it

agree: Use waking mind time to feed work to background mind
notes: Abstractions are strategy: “you are making some super global decision that is going to need to be correct in a whole bunch of contexts in which you cannot make tactical decisions yet.”
So the hammock is where Simple Made Easy's “simplify the problem space before you start” gets done.

slides.title: Feeding the background mind

runs.caption: Looked at it for ten minutes, then went to the movies.
Load it up: write it all down, go over it in different orders, then close your eyes.
Wait for it — at least overnight. Then pick it apart while awake.

slides.caption: You did not think about it hard enough while you were awake for it to become important to your mind when you are asleep.
notes: “if you can imagine having an assistant who every now and then can take one of those out and put a different color in, then you could juggle balls of 20 different colors at the same time as long as there are only nine in the air at any one point in time.”
The notes are that assistant.

slides.title: Wait for it, then try it

items.text: At least overnight
sub: “sleep sober for best results”

items.text: Work on more than one thing — not within a day, but over time
sub: “Don't stay stuck. Switch.”

items.text: Wake up working
sub: sometimes with the answer to a different problem — capture it

items.text: Eventually, coding is required — type sparingly
sub: “if I think that I have got an answer and the answer is small, that is one of the most telling attributes that it is probably good.”

items.text: Feedback loops matter, but don't lean on them
sub: “Test-driven dentistry, I do not think I could come up with a better thing.”

slides.notes: “It can take between an hour and an entire day to load up something, so once you have done that, you try to get at least the rest of the day, or three days, or more on it.”

slides.quote: If I could advocate anything, it is "Do not be afraid" especially, "do not be afraid of being wrong."
notes: “When the facts change, do not dig in.”
The summary slide: “It's a rant! it doesn't have a summary”.

slides.title: Two definitions of complexity

left.name: Ousterhout
points: Whatever makes a system hard to understand and modify
Measured by its symptoms: change amplification, cognitive load, unknown unknowns
Caused by dependencies and obscurity
Hide it in deep modules

right.name: Hickey
points: Braiding: things interleaved that could be independent
Objective: look for the braids
Caused by complecting constructs: state, objects, syntax…
Don't hide it: avoid it — values, data, functions, queues

slides.notes: Ousterhout's definition is about the reader (closer to Hickey's “hard”); Hickey's is about the structure. They mostly point at the same code.

slides.title: The same idea, again

items.text: “I don't know, I don't want to know” ≈ information hiding
“Partitioning doesn't imply simplicity” ≈ the flowchart decomposition: modular, but sharing every decision
Incidental ≈ accidental complexity
“State is never simple” ≈ state as the major cause
The simplicity toolkit ≈ functional relational programming: values, declarative data, rules

slides.notes: The Tar Pit's FRP split — essential state as relations, logic as pure functions, control and performance separated — is Hickey's right-hand column almost item by item.

slides.title: Where they pull apart

items.text: Hide information, or expose it?
sub: Ousterhout hides design decisions inside deep classes
Hickey: Represent data as data — hide how, never the facts

items.text: Fewer things, or more?
sub: Ousterhout warns about classitis — many shallow classes
Hickey: more things, as long as they hang straight — he counts braids, not parts

items.text: Objects
sub: APOSD's examples are classes; to Hickey objects complect state, identity and value
the Tar Pit sides with Hickey: OOP tightly couples state together with related behaviour

slides.notes: One way to reconcile them: both want small interfaces over a lot of hidden “how”. They disagree about whether information itself belongs behind an interface.

slides.title: Easy, mistaken for simple
slides.subtitle: this week's exercise, with public examples
slides.notes: The task asks for three places in your own code. These are public ones so the deck can be shared; bring your own to the discussion.

slides.title: 1 · java.util.Date: a value that was a place

panes.label: java.util.Date (1996)
code: // standup has moved an hour too:
// it kept a reference to the same place

panes.label: java.time (Java 8, 2014)
code: // start is a value: standup is unchanged
// and later is a new fact

steps.caption: Easy: one mutable class, at hand in every JDK since 1.0.
Complected: the date and the moment you read it.
Simple: immutable values, new values for new facts.

notes: The cost of untangling: a second date/time API (JSR 310), and two decades of code that still passes Dates around. Effective Java's “make defensive copies” item uses this exact class.
Name the braid: value and time. Easy in which sense: at hand and familiar.

slides.title: 2 · Array.prototype.sort: easy, and in place

steps.caption: sort returns the array it was given — after changing it.
toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced and with return new arrays.

notes: The cost of untangling: sort can never change (the web depends on it), so the language grew a second set of methods.
Name the braid: the result and the input — and, through any other reference to the array, everyone else's view of it.

slides.title: 3 · Lisp's parens (Hickey's own)

items.text: Easy to describe: everything is a list
Complected: one construct for calls, grouping and data
Clojure's fix: more data structures — vectors, maps, sets
The cost: a new language, not a patch

slides.notes: Hickey's own example from Simple Made Easy. In all three cases the braid could not be undone in place: the old thing stays, and the simple version lives next to it. That is what untangling costs once others depend on the braid.
